newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore bank loans growth to fall in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Singapore bank loans growth to fall in 1997.

text.p: Singapore banks are finding it more and more difficult to lend money and will see loans growth squeezed over the next year as the current economic slowdown begins to bite, analysts said on Thursday.

Total lending by Singapore banks to non-bank customers is expected to rise by between 14 and 15 percent to around Singapore $125 billion (US$89.3 billion) at the end of 1996, compared with an expansion of 19.8 percent in 1995.
Loans growth in 1997 is expected to fall to just 10-12 percent year-on-year, they said.
"Next year will be a lot tougher for the local banking sector," said Lim Eng Hai, head of research at Singapore brokerage J.M. Sassoon.
"We haven't yet really seen the effects of the recent slowdown in manufacturing or the lower property market reaching the banks," he said.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Thursday bank credit was 16.4 percent greater year-on-year in September, compared with 17.4 percent annual growth in August.
"The slowdown was broad-based. Growth of loans to the manufacturing and building and construction sector eased," the MAS said in its monthly bulletin.
Manufacturing loans grew 12.6 percent in September, from 13 percent in August, while building and construction credit expanded by 22.6 percent, from 22.9 percent the month before.
The most obvious slowdown in lending was for customers of finance houses which saw loans increase just 1.4 percent year-on-year in September, after a rise of three percent year-on-year in August.
"This largely reflected the 15 percent fall in hire-purchase financing, as lending for motor-vehicle purchases declined further," the MAS said.
Analysts said the fall in loans growth could be attributed partly to the economic slowdown in Singapore this year as a result of the slump in the global electronics industry.
Electronics account for almost half Singapore's industrial production and about 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
Singapore's economy is expected to grow by about six percent this year from 8.8 percent in 1995 and 10.2 percent in 1994.
But some bank loans, particularly those to industry, see a lag of up to two years between initial approval and drawdown.
"That time-lag means the impact of the slowdown is still in the pipeline. So the 16 percent increase in September understates the current slowdown," Lim said.
He said the effect of government measures in May of this year to curb speculation in the island's property market had also still to show up in the figures.
Singapore banks would need to look to overseas loans to make up for the more competitive home environment, analysts said.

But given the long lag times of some loans, Singapore banks should be able to ride out the economic slowdown, particularly if it was short-lived, said William Cliffe, institutional dealer at the securities arm of the Development Bank of Singapore Ltd .

"Singapore banks will still see the drawing in 1998 of some loan commitments made before the slowdown," he said. "By then the economy will have picked up again and there should be very healthy growth in demand for new credit."
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703199)
